sections.content: The course covers all the core calculus topics clearly, starting from the basics of limits and derivatives, moving through differentiation rules, applications like optimization, and ending with integrals and their uses. The content builds step by step, so even if you’re a bit rusty with high school math, you can keep up as long as you follow the lectures. It’s a solid foundation for any student who needs calculus for their major, and the examples given are practical enough to help you understand how the concepts work, not just memorize formulas.
sections.teaching: The professor is really patient and explains every concept in detail. They go through each example slowly, breaking down the steps so you can follow along easily. They also encourage questions during and after class, and always take the time to re-explain tricky parts. Even when the material gets a bit more complex, they use simple analogies and extra practice problems to make it less intimidating. The lectures are well-structured, and the pace is steady—you just need to stay focused and take notes to keep up.
sections.grading: The grading is fair and transparent. The exams and assignments follow the style taught in class, and partial credit is given for showing your work, which is really helpful if you make small mistakes. The midterm and final are straightforward, with questions that test both understanding and application, rather than just trick questions. The curve is applied fairly, so your grade reflects how well you keep up with the course, not just how you compare to everyone else.
sections.workload: The workload is balanced and manageable for a first-year math course. There are regular problem sets that help you practice what you learn, and they’re not overly long—just enough to keep you on track. The midterm and final require some review, but since the material builds gradually, you won’t have to cram everything at the last minute. Overall, as long as you keep up with the weekly practice and go over the lecture notes, the workload won’t feel overwhelming.

sections.content:
This course covers the fundamental knowledge of derivative securities, which it is very important to have relevant knowledge in the finance industry. The course discuss a wide range of applications, such as the use of derivatives, how to price the derivatives, what are the intuition behind those derivatives etc.
For the details of the lecture chapters pls refers to other reviews.
sections.teaching: Prof. Yan Ji is a very patient prof where you can often see him stay behind after class to ans students' questions. Also, he always use a lot of examples/ intuitions to explain some complex concepts of derivatives, which it helps a lot for you to understand the reason behind the pricing of certain derivatives and how are they being used in real life. He always stress the word "intuitions" in class as he wants us to understand the concept, not just memories them. However, I have to say the way he teaches may seems a little fast and a bit hard to follow at first if you don't have too much understanding of the concepts beforehand just like me, which you need to watch the recordings back a couple times and jot down notes so that you can better prepare and revise for the exams. But once you watch the recordings back and understand the concepts, all of a sudden everything he said would makes a lot of sense. He's defo one of the best prof in ust.
sections.grading:
The grading is not bad at all I have to say, even tho the curve are extremely steep, I am certain he already gave 25% A range (maximum allowed) to students so you can't really complain abt that (it's the stupid sch policy at the end of the day)
Here are some of my stats for my semester:

Asm 15%: full
Attendance 10%: full
Midterm 25%: 95/100 (mean 85, median 87)
Final exam 50%: 96/120
Overall: 88.75% (A-)

You don't actually need to get all the ans completely correct in the asm and even exams as the marking schemes stated that as long as the students shows their workings and shows their understanding of the questions to a certain extent, you will get full marks for that questions, which is very nice. A lot of the questions in midterm and final actually test your understanding of the concepts more than mathematical calculations.

As you can see, A range is actually not that wide when you compare with others' stats, where 86% being B+ while 94% is A+, but it's all down to the competiveness of this course that led to such steep curve.

Ps. I spent too much time in some of the questions in the beginning in final and led to me not being able to finish all questions and lost some crucial marks, but getting an A- is already more than satisfactory for me.
sections.workload: The workload is not too high, I would say it's medium, with 5 asms, 1 midterm and 1 final, there're also 1 optional asm for you to practice for your own good. Prof Yan Ji also gave some past exam paper for you to revise both the midterm and final as well which is pretty nice

sections.content:
Before mid-term: Forwards, futures, different kind of swaps.
After mid-term: Different options, credit derivatives

For me, I am not good at replicating portfolio so swaps had given me a hard time. Better spend more time on understanding the replication technique if you are not good at doing reverse engineering stuff.

Post mid-term stuff:
Introduction to options
Pricing options: Binomial tree, BSM
Option properties: Relationship of option prices w.r.t Time to maturity, underlying's volatility, even dividend of underlying is considered.
Introduction of some exotic options
Credit derivatives

The post mt stuff are more challenging in terms of the math and computation. Such as the BSM formula, which  I think involve PDE in its derivation. You don't need to know how to derive for exam purpose, but interpreting some terms like delta is required.

The credit derivatives part is a little bit rushed. We are given some formulas to calculate probability of default but few intuition is given.

For exam, remember to have BSM formula on your cheat sheet. Although professor says he does not test you on computation, the exam actually involve at least 8(?) times of computing option price, with different parameters each time! So getting familiar with the formula is also important.
sections.teaching: Focus on intuition and logic. He makes use of simple graphs instead of equations to explain concepts, which helps learning.

sections.content:
Mainly 4 parts of derivatives are introduced by Prof Ji:
--- Midterm ---
1. Forwards and Futures
Forwards & futures of commodities, dividend-paying stocks, interests and currencies, their pricing with arbitrage strategies.
2. Swaps
Swaps as an extension of normal forwards.
--- Final (Non-cumulative) ---
3. Options
European vs American options, binomial tree pricing, risk-neutral pricing, exotics, theoretical results and empirical issues of BSM.
4. Credits
Credits and credit derivatives.
sections.teaching:
Well, what's important is the philosophy.
Remember in this course, the philosophy is arbitrage strategy. This includes arbitrage tables, risk neutral pricing as a corollary of non-arbitrage conditions and binomial trees.
Prof Ji teaches you both philosophy and some new issues of research so he is really fantastic. Meanwhile, he is very organized!
However, content-wise the course is very heavy and detailed so he prepares both exam and non-exam versions. I would say much essence and insights are shared in non-exam - but it doesn't mean he will test them. So he is generous and kind simultaneously as a professor :)
sections.grading:
HW + Midterm + Final + Attendance.
--- Midterm ---
Mean is around 80+, normally sd is high such that if you get full marks you are likely just above 1 sd. I feel they grade your paper on your effort and methods, not on your accuracy so you do have a room for mistakes, this is very nice (I feel they are even generous in some sense of grading the midterm)
They didn't test every topic but don't make a bet on it.
--- Final ---
OK, so this year they took 20 days to give you final grade, that is super rare so people should be patient enough... You know, the final is on 29th May but they release the grade after summer term starts, that is insane.
They claim they hired 2 TAs to grade your paper 3 times, I feel "man what can I say" but they should grade your work very fairly.
No statistics are given but you have a chance to see your grade of final (I guess they released mistakenly for a while)
The paper was very calculation-wise heavy. Don't grind on single questions.
-------
My results: Midterm 100/100, Final 100+/120 -> A+
I feel the grade is good enough but I only have myself as a sample so it might be kinda biased!

It is a giant ZERO.
5 problem sets with probably 3 graded questions. Rest of problem sets are optional. By optional they are indeed optional i.e. they are not covered by exam versions of the slides (This is so fair and nice in terms of reducing your workload)

sections.content:
This course covers one of the most exciting yet fundamental areas in finance: derivative securities. The global derivatives market is one of the most fast-growing markets, with over $600 trillion notional value in total. In the modern financial architecture, financial derivatives can be the most challenging and exotic securities traded by institutional specialists, while at the same time, they can also be the basic securities commonly traded by retail investors such as S&P 500 Index Options. Beyond trading, the basic ideas of financial derivatives serve as building blocks to understand a much broader class of financial problems, such as complex asset portfolios, strategic corporate decisions, and stages in venture capital investing. Therefore, It is as important as ever to understand both the strategic opportunities offered by these derivative instruments and the risks they imply.

We discuss a wide range of applications, including the use of derivatives in asset management, the valuation of corporate securities such as stocks and corporate bonds with embedded options, interest rate derivatives, credit derivatives, as well as crude oil derivatives. In addition to theoretical discussions,
we also emphasize practical considerations of implementing strategies using derivatives as tools, especially when no-arbitrage conditions do not hold.

Topic 1: Introduction to Derivatives
L1 - Introduction to Derivatives

Topic 2: Forwards and Futures
L2 - Forward and Futures contracts
L3 - Forwards and Futures on commodities
L4 - Forwards and Futures on currencies
L5 - Forwards and Futures on interest rates

Topic 3: Swaps
L6 - Swaps

Topic 4: Options Basics
L7 - Introduction to options
L8 - Option Trading Strategies

Topic 5: Binomial Trees
L9 - Binomial Tree Models
L10 - Multi-step Binomial Tree Models

Topic 6: Black-Scholes-Merton model

L12 - Delta Hedging in the BSM Model
L13 - Some issues with the BSM Model

Topic 7: Exotic options and Default
L14 - American and Exotic Options
L15 - Default modeling and credit derivatives

So, rather than memorizing examples in ppt or homework, it is more useful to really understand the intuition behind as exam questions won't be exactly the same as those in the ppt or homework.

sections.teaching:
A good (and young?) professor for this course since he himself is a trader. Andrew has an Engineering degree but switched to the Finance field in his further studies.

He can speak English very fluently and can communicate well with both local and non-local students. He always tried his best to explain the concepts to students using examples (with the aid of his tablet and excel).

The pace of teaching was also fine. Andrew did not only spend time quickly going through the slides. In many of his lectures, he told us real-life trading things (not tested) so if you are interested in trading you will be very happy to listen. He also told jokes frequently to make the lectures less intense.

You can ask Andrew questions anonymously on the website he provided and he will reply them in Canvas announcements. He was also very nice that he gave us hints before the two exams

Lecture videos were uploaded to Canvas, but the people who recorded them sometimes did not catch up the screens timely.

In my opinion, for those who have no idea what derivatives are before taking this course (like me), what calls and puts are, it will be a bit hard for you to catch up.

sections.content:
This course is quite quantitative but  easy. You do not need to worry too much before enrolling into this course.

Ch1 Introduction to Derivatives
Ch2 Mechanics of Future Markets
Ch3 Hedging Strategies
Ch4 Interest Rate
Ch5 Forward Futures Price
Ch6 Swaps
Ch7 Option Price Properties
Ch8 Option Strategies
Ch9 Binomial Option Pricing
Ch10 Black-Scholes Model
Ch11 Applications of Black-Scholes Formula
Ch12 Greek Letters Risks

Midterm tests up to topic 5, and it is non-cumulative. Most of the content are related to calculations but you also need to understand the concepts as professor tests more on understanding in exams.
sections.teaching: Professor's teaching is normal and sometimes too slow at the beginning of the course. It makes topic 12 not covered in final exam as there is not enough time to talk about this topic. I only attend the first lesson and watch the lecture videos for all the remaining lessons.
sections.grading:
The grading of Sophie is very very good.

Midterm 40%
Final Exam 40%
Homework X 2 20%

I get full marks in both pieces of homework. midterm higher than mean 0.8 sd, and final mark is unknown.

Finally, the grade is A.
sections.workload: The workload is quite low for this course. Although there is suggested questions in syllabus, i do not recommend you to do all the questions in the textbook as the questions you find in exams will not be the type in textbook. In exams, most of the questions are not about calculations, but other types of questions such as proof and explanations. So you need to 100% understand the content in lecture notes so that you can master the exam's questions.

sections.content:

5 assignment. If you listen to the teaching carefully & discuss with friends, they are not very challenging. However, they are time-consuming. You might have to spend 2~ 5 hours for each of them. But adequate time is given.

2 exams. If you understand what is taught then you may just need 2~3 days to prepare for each exam.
